newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Greenspan opposed to mixing banking, commerce.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Greenspan opposed to mixing banking, commerce.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan Thursday criticised proposed legislation to overhaul U.S. banking laws, saying the bill goes too far in allowing banks to own or be owned by automakers or other companies.
Greenspan said he supported the overall thrust of the proposal, which would tear down the legal barriers separating banking from other financial service industries.
But the central bank chief said he strongly opposed a controversial part of the bill that would allow banks to get into completely unrelated businesses like manufacturing or health care.

The bill "goes well beyond what both commercial banks and non-financial firms need to meet the requirements of today, as well as in the foreseeable future," Greenspan told a subcommittee of the House Commerce Committee.
The Commerce Committee has until mid-September to complete its work on the bank reform bill, which passed 28-26 in a House Banking Committee vote last month.

Even if the committee approves a bill, the legislation faces an uncertain fate. Congress has been trying for more than a decade to reform the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act as part of an overhaul of ageing financial regulations.

The banking and commerce provisions are considered critical to garner the support of the securities and insurance industries, analysts said. Companies in those industries already own commodities firms, manufacturers and real estate assets, among others, and want to be able to buy banks without having to divest those businesses.

Greenspan said the Fed recognised that the line between banking and commerce was already eroding and eventually will disappear, but said regulators should move cautiously in knocking down the legal barriers that now separate the two.

"Current facts and future trends, in short, are creating market pressures to permit common ownership," Greenspan said. But caution is warranted "since the unrestricted association of banking and commerce would be a profound and surely irreversible structural change in the American economy."

If the bill became law in its present form, a financial company that owned a bank could derive up to 15 percent of its revenue from commercial activity but could not affiliate with a commercial company that had assets of more than $750 million.
A commercial company could also derive up to 15 percent of its revenue from banking but could not own a bank with more than $500 million in assets.
Greenspan said the 15 percent limit was much too large, but he declined to specify a preferred limit. "As that basket gets smaller and smaller, I would feel better and better," he said.
At least one other bank regulator agreed with Greenspan. Andrew Hove, acting director of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp., said the 15 percent level should be lowered to 5 percent.
"A 15-percent-of-revenue basket may allow too much to happen too fast," he told lawmakers at the hearing. Five percent "would be a prudent starting point."
